definition: Exogenous means caused by factors from outside a system rather than from within it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word exogenous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know exogenous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The lake's sudden algae bloom was exogenous, fed by fertilizer washing in from farms miles upstream.
Outside simply says where something is located, while exogenous makes a stronger claim: that a system's change was driven by forces beyond its own borders.
An exogenous factor comes from outside a system, but an invasive one goes further, pushing its way in and actively disrupting what it finds.

External means coming from the outside, and it fits anything at all — external walls, external pressure, an external hard drive. Exogenous is the analyst's word: it classifies a cause as originating beyond the system under study, usually in deliberate contrast with a homegrown one. Street noise is external; a currency shock is exogenous.

Extrinsic means originating outside a thing's essential nature — extrinsic motivation comes from prizes and grades, not love of the work. Exogenous is about systems and causes: a force from beyond a system's borders driving change inside it. Extrinsic contrasts with what something is; exogenous contrasts with what a system does to itself.

Oxygen was coined as the 'acid-producer' -- Greek oxys ('sharp, acid') plus the same gen- root of origin and birth that sits inside exogenous -- because early chemists believed the gas gave birth to every acid.
Exogenous means caused by factors from outside a system rather than from within it.
For decades, a mountain town's ski economy ran on steady snow and loyal visitors.
Then a national airline canceled the only direct route into the regional airport, a decision made at a headquarters two thousand miles away.
Bookings collapsed within a single season even though the snow, the lodges, and the service were as good as ever.
The slump was exogenous: nothing inside the town's own economy had changed at all.
The downturn was caused entirely by an outside force, a distant airline's decision, not by anything within the town's own economic system, which is what exogenous means.
formal, academic/scientific register
Exogenous appears in economics, medicine, and ecology to label causes that originate outside the system being studied (an exogenous shock, an exogenous infection).
Its direct antonym is endogenous, caused from within; asking whether a change is exogenous or endogenous is asking whether the trouble came from outside or was homegrown.

For two seasons the valley's orchardists blamed themselves for the blight: too little pruning, tired soil, thin spraying.
The extension office sent a plant pathologist, who sampled every affected row and mapped the infections by date.
Her verdict reversed the story: the outbreak was exogenous, arriving on imported nursery stock and spreading outward from the two farms that had planted it.
Orchards that had bought no new trees stayed clean, however carelessly they pruned.
The distinction changed the remedy overnight -- no amount of soil care would help, but a quarantine on incoming stock might.
